title: Stem before leaves
subtitle: Find the plant's main movement.
idea: A stem is a route through the drawing. Establish its bends and the attachment points before surrounding it with leaves. A flexible plant rarely follows a ruler-straight axis; its changes of direction organize the whole study.
observation: Follow the fern from its base to the tip. The small leaves belong to a shared structure rather than floating independently.
steps: Draw the main stem as one slow gesture.
Place only the attachment points and short leaf directions.
Hide the guide and rebuild the branch from its rhythm.
check: Do the leaves feel connected to one growing structure?
transfer: Draw the gesture of a real herb sprig before its outline.

title: A leaf inside an envelope
subtitle: Simplify before describing.
idea: An envelope is a small set of straight edges that contains a curved form. It gives you a width, height, and tilt to check before the contour becomes complicated. Correct the envelope while it is still light.
observation: Compare one broad leaf with a narrow one. Their widest points occur at different distances from their tips.
steps: Choose one leaf and mark its tip and base.
Join four straight segments around its outer boundary.
Fade the image and fit a continuous contour inside that boundary.
check: Did the width and tilt survive the refinement?
transfer: Block in three leaves from a plant using four lines each.

title: The gaps between leaves
subtitle: Draw the air around a plant.
idea: Negative shapes have angles and proportions of their own. Comparing those unfamiliar shapes can interrupt the habit of drawing a memorized leaf symbol. A convincing gap often fixes both neighboring leaves at once.
observation: Look at a triangular opening between two branches and a narrow slit between neighboring leaves.
steps: Outline three empty gaps without drawing leaf veins.
Connect the plant edges that enclose those gaps.
Hide the reference and invent a branch with three different gaps.
check: Are my gaps varied rather than evenly stamped?
transfer: Sketch the spaces in a kitchen whisk or a wire basket.

title: Leaves that turn away
subtitle: Notice the narrowing surface.
idea: A leaf turning away presents a smaller visible surface. Compare its apparent width with its length instead of assuming that every leaf has the same shape. Its central vein can help you track the turn.
observation: Some leaves show broad faces while others narrow toward an edge. Compare their visible widths along their central directions.
steps: Choose a broad leaf and a narrower neighboring one.
Draw both central directions and compare their widths.
Reconstruct the pair with a faint guide, keeping their different tilts.
check: Can I tell which leaf turns away from me?
transfer: Turn a real leaf in your hand and sketch three viewpoints.

title: Hatching a green surface
subtitle: Turn color into value.
idea: Green does not have to become a single dark patch. Look for the light and shadow within each leaf, then choose a small group of values. Curved hatches can describe the surface without outlining every vein.
observation: Compare the lit leaf edges with darker overlaps. Small veins are less important than the broad light pattern.
steps: Draw one leaf lightly and leave its brightest strip empty.
Curve a few hatches from the central vein toward the edge.
Hide the guide and describe a second leaf using only three values.
check: Do the hatches help the leaf turn in space?
transfer: Draw a real leaf in monochrome under one lamp.

title: A flower seen at an angle
subtitle: Build the disk before the petals.
idea: A flower head can be organized around a tilted disk. The visible disk becomes narrower as it turns away, while the petals overlap around it. This is a starting structure, not a rule that every flower is perfectly circular.
observation: Compare the forward-facing cosmos with a flower tilted sideways. Their centers and petal spreads have different proportions.
steps: Mark the center and tilt of each flower head.
Sketch a light ellipse around each spread of petals.
Fade the guide and place the petals around those ellipses.
check: Do the heads face different directions?
transfer: Draw the same simple flower from above and from the side.

title: Petals in front and behind
subtitle: Let overlap explain depth.
idea: Overlapping petals create small T-shaped junctions: one edge stops where another passes in front. Draw the front edge continuously and allow the hidden edge to stop. A dark outline around every petal can flatten the flower.
observation: Find a petal that covers its neighbor. Notice the edge that continues and the edge that disappears.
steps: Choose three overlapping petals and draw the nearest first.
Stop the rear contours where they become hidden.
Hide the guide and invent a small cluster with the same overlap order.
check: Can I name which petal is nearest without shading?
transfer: Arrange three paper scraps and sketch their overlaps.

title: Stems through a glass
subtitle: Separate what you see from what you expect.
idea: Transparent objects mix visible contours, reflections, and displaced views of what lies behind them. Draw the shapes actually visible through the glass. Avoid forcing the stems into perfectly continuous lines when the image shows an offset.
observation: The glass rim, water boundary, and stems make several distinct edges. Keep them separate rather than drawing one heavy cylinder.
steps: Lightly establish the outer glass and its rim.
Locate only the visible stem segments inside it.
Add two or three reflected light shapes, leaving most glass unshaded.
check: Does the glass feel transparent rather than metallic?
transfer: Observe a spoon in a real glass of water without assuming its shape.

title: A bouquet in three values
subtitle: Group the light before the detail.
idea: A tonal plan reduces a complex subject to a few large families. White petals can remain mostly paper while dark background gaps describe their edges. Preserve the shared light pattern before selecting any petal veins.
observation: Squint at the flowers, glass, and background. Separate the brightest petals, middle stems, and darker spaces.
steps: Make three small value swatches beside your study.
Block the bouquet as large connected light and dark shapes.
Fade the guide and add detail to only one flower head.
check: Does the bouquet still read when viewed small?
transfer: Photograph a bouquet you own and simplify it to three values.

title: A botanical page of your own
subtitle: Combine structure and selective detail.
idea: A study page can explain how a plant works without rendering every part equally. Combine an overall gesture, one enlarged detail, and a small memory drawing. Changing scale makes the page more informative than a single laborious copy.
observation: Compare the fern's repeated growth with the cosmos arrangement. Choose the plant whose structure interests you most.
steps: Draw one small whole-plant study from the reference.
Enlarge one leaf or petal and describe its turning surface.
Hide the guide and make a memory sketch; write what changed.
check: Does each drawing on my page have a different purpose?
transfer: Make the same three-part page from a plant near your home.

title: Two pears, two silhouettes
subtitle: Look past the label of the object.
idea: Two objects with the same name can have very different boundaries. Compare the shoulder width, lean, and low bulge of each pear. An irregular silhouette usually carries more character than decorative spots.
observation: One pear stands while the other rests at a different angle. Their stems do not point in the same direction.
steps: Mark each pear's top, bottom, and widest points.
Connect those landmarks with a light angular envelope.
Fade the guide and refine only the contours that change direction.
check: Can I distinguish the two pears by outline alone?
transfer: Draw two real pieces of fruit without any interior marks.

title: A shared measuring unit
subtitle: Compare objects on the same table.
idea: Choose a visible length, such as the cup's width, and use it to compare the entire arrangement. Relative measurements keep the drawing coherent even when you change its overall size. Recheck the gaps as well as the objects.
observation: Compare a pear's height with the cup opening and the interval between them. Do not measure each object in isolation.
steps: Mark the total width of the arrangement.
Place the cup, bottle, and apple using one repeated unit.
Hide the guide and redraw the arrangement at half the size.
check: Do the ratios remain similar in my smaller version?
transfer: Compare three objects using the smallest object's height as a unit.

title: Shadows that share a light
subtitle: Ground the whole arrangement.
idea: Cast shadows connect an object to a surface. Start with their broad direction, then locate the darker contact area near the object. Under one dominant light, the separate shadows should make a consistent spatial story.
observation: The pears and cup receive light from the same side. Look for the dark contact shapes beneath them and softer outer shadow edges.
steps: Outline the broad cast-shadow shapes lightly.
Darken only the contact areas closest to the objects.
Fade the guide and connect objects and shadows into one study.
check: Do my shadows suggest one consistent light direction?
transfer: Place two objects beside a lamp and compare their shadows.

title: Lose an edge on purpose
subtitle: Let value carry the boundary.
idea: A lost edge occurs where neighboring values become similar. You can allow part of a contour to disappear while preserving enough information elsewhere. This selective description directs attention and avoids a cutout effect.
observation: Find a pear edge that is strongly separated from its background and another with a gentler transition.
steps: Draw the high-contrast portion of one silhouette.
Build the neighboring values and leave one quiet edge incomplete.
Hide the image and test whether the pear still feels whole.
check: Did I choose which edges deserve emphasis?
transfer: Draw a pale object against a pale cloth with only half its contour.

title: Folds as a sequence of planes
subtitle: Simplify the cloth under the objects.
idea: A fold turns a surface toward or away from light. Start with the largest ridge and valley rather than copying the fabric weave. Broad value changes describe a fold; tiny texture belongs only after that structure reads.
observation: Follow the cloth from a raised ridge down to a shadowed valley. Notice where its edge overlaps itself.
steps: Draw three major fold directions.
Assign a light, middle, or dark value to each broad plane.
Fade the guide and add a few texture marks near one ridge only.
check: Do my values explain the fold before the weave does?
transfer: Drape a towel over a book and draw its three largest planes.

title: The pitcher's tilted opening
subtitle: Align the rim with the vessel.
idea: A rim needs a center, a tilt, and a believable opening. Compare its long axis with the vessel's center direction. The rim's inner and outer edges describe thickness, so they should work together rather than become unrelated ovals.
observation: Look at the pitcher's mouth and the bowl's opening. They are both circular objects seen from an angle but their visible shapes differ.
steps: Draw a light center direction through the pitcher.
Place the outer opening and then the visible inner lip.
Fade the image and join the rim to the body without sharp corners.
check: Does my rim belong to the same vessel as the body?
transfer: Sketch a jug opening from two eye levels.

title: The space inside a handle
subtitle: Build the hole before the handle.
idea: The handle's opening is often easier to compare than its familiar outer shape. Establish that negative space first, then build the surrounding thickness. Where the handle meets the vessel, overlap and shadow explain the connection.
observation: Compare the opening's height and width. Notice that the handle does not have identical thickness at every point.
steps: Draw the empty handle opening as a simple shape.
Build the outer handle around it.
Hide the guide and attach a new handle to an invented vessel.
check: Is the opening convincing before I shade the handle?
transfer: Draw a real mug handle by beginning with its empty space.

title: A bowl has thickness
subtitle: Show the edge that turns inward.
idea: A bowl is more than an ellipse above a curve. Its rim has thickness, and its inner surface turns away from the viewer. Reserve a narrow light edge when you need to distinguish the rim from the darker interior.
observation: Compare the dark bowl interior with its lighter lip and the shadow beneath the base.
steps: Block in the bowl's overall width and depth.
Draw the inner opening and preserve the visible rim.
Fade the guide and separate interior, exterior, and cast shadow.
check: Can I tell where the surface turns into the bowl?
transfer: Observe an empty bowl from above before drawing its side view.

title: Glaze without overworking
subtitle: Describe a surface with selective contrast.
idea: A glossy or glazed surface may show a compact reflection while the underlying form still needs broad shading. Keep the highlight simple, and do not scatter equally bright marks everywhere. The value structure should remain readable without the highlight.
observation: The blue bowl and matte pitcher respond differently to light. Compare the size and sharpness of their light patches.
steps: Draw both objects using three broad values.
Reserve the reflected window shape on the green jug and a softer light area on the matte cup.
Hide the guide and check which surface feels glossier.
check: Do the reflections support the form rather than interrupt it?
transfer: Compare a glazed cup and an unglazed pot under the same light.

title: A quiet still-life composition
subtitle: Make a deliberate arrangement.
idea: Composition begins with choices about scale, space, and overlap. Compare a close crop with a spacious arrangement before committing. A finished study needs an intention, not the maximum possible number of objects.
observation: Look at the gap between the pitcher and bowl. Consider how that interval changes the balance of the whole frame.
steps: Make two thumbnails with different amounts of empty space.
Choose one and place the large object shapes.
Fade the guide and finish only the focal area; reflect on your choice.
check: Can I explain why I chose this crop?
transfer: Arrange two household objects and draw three composition thumbnails.

title: Follow the shell's growth
subtitle: Organize a spiral without a formula.
idea: A shell spiral changes its spacing as it grows. Observe the visible turns rather than forcing every curve into a perfectly even decorative pattern. Place the large outer envelope before studying the smaller center.
observation: Compare the tight inner turns with the broader outer sweep. Look for where the spiral becomes partly hidden.
steps: Draw the shell's outer envelope and center location.
Trace the visible growth direction in a few broad curves.
Fade the guide and rebuild the spiral with fewer lines.
check: Does my spiral grow rather than repeat at one size?
transfer: Sketch the growth directions in a real shell or rolled leaf.

title: The opening is a shape
subtitle: Look into the shell's aperture.
idea: The aperture is a negative shape with a boundary, tilt, and depth. Establish its silhouette before darkening it. A uniform black hole can hide useful information about the lip and interior planes.
observation: The opening is bordered by a brighter lip and darker recess. Compare its long direction with the whole shell.
steps: Draw the opening as an empty flat shape.
Add the outer shell around it and locate the visible lip.
Fade the reference and use two values to suggest its depth.
check: Is the opening placed correctly before the dark value is added?
transfer: Draw the opening of a pitcher or curled paper tube.

title: Ridges that wrap around
subtitle: Make texture obey the larger form.
idea: Repeated ridges can explain curvature when their spacing and direction follow the surface. They can also flatten it if treated as parallel decoration. Begin with just a few structural ridges and leave room for the form's shading.
observation: Notice how ridge directions turn across the shell and how some vanish around its far side.
steps: Draw the shell with a light outline.
Place five major ridges that follow the visible curvature.
Hide the guide and add tone between selected ridges, leaving quiet areas.
check: Do my ridges wrap around the shell?
transfer: Draw grooves in a real onion skin or a ribbed bottle.

title: A thin edge, a solid object
subtitle: Use thickness to explain material.
idea: Even a thin shell has thickness where its surface turns toward an opening. A narrow band of light or shadow can suggest that edge. Avoid making every visible boundary equally heavy; thickness is a spatial relationship.
observation: Study the lip beside the aperture. Compare it with the broader shadowed body rather than isolating it as an outline.
steps: Place the lip's two boundaries lightly.
Shade the inside and outside as different planes.
Fade the guide and keep only the marks needed to describe the edge.
check: Can I see where the surface turns inward?
transfer: Fold a piece of thick paper and draw the edge of the fold.

title: A shell from memory
subtitle: Test the relationships you noticed.
idea: Memory drawing reveals which large relationships you observed. It does not require perfect recall of every ridge. Compare your reconstruction with the reference and choose one specific adjustment instead of labeling the entire drawing wrong.
observation: Keep the center, outer sweep, and opening as your three main anchors.
steps: Study the reference and draw only its three anchors.
Switch to Freehand and rebuild the shell without tracing.
Reveal the image and mark one proportion you would revise.
check: Which relationship survived, and which needs another look?
transfer: Repeat the method with a small object from your desk.

title: A pebble has planes
subtitle: Find structure in a rounded surface.
idea: A rounded stone may contain flatter patches separated by gentle turns. Group those patches into a few value planes. The aim is to explain the stone's mass before adding speckles or cracks.
observation: Compare the broad lit plane of the largest pebble with its darker side. The boundary is softer than a cut cube's edge.
steps: Draw one stone's outer envelope.
Divide its surface into three broad value areas.
Fade the image and connect the areas with a few softer transitions.
check: Does the stone feel solid without texture?
transfer: Light a real pebble from one side and draw three planes.

title: Overlap a small collection
subtitle: Arrange depth without perspective lines.
idea: When one stone covers another, the interrupted contour gives a strong depth cue. Contact shadows can strengthen that relationship. Keep the individual stones' shapes clear before joining their tones into a group.
observation: Find a place where one pebble hides part of another. Compare that overlap with a pair separated by a gap.
steps: Draw the nearest pebble first.
Add the visible portions of the stones behind it.
Hide the guide and invent a new three-stone arrangement.
check: Is the front-to-back order unambiguous?
transfer: Arrange three small objects and sketch their contour interruptions.

title: Dark stone, light stone
subtitle: Separate local value from lighting.
idea: A dark object in light can remain darker than a pale object in shadow. Compare the objects as a group rather than assigning the same light and shadow values to every surface. Squinting helps you simplify the relationship.
observation: Compare the black basalt with the white marble. Both have light and shadow, but their overall value ranges differ.
steps: Make two short value scales for the two stones.
Draw the large shapes using the appropriate value family.
Fade the reference and preserve the difference while adding shadows.
check: Do the stones keep their different local values?
transfer: Draw a black mug beside a white mug under the same lamp.

title: Suggest texture, leave silence
subtitle: Choose a few telling marks.
idea: Texture reads through contrast with quieter areas. A handful of cracks or flecks can describe a stone more clearly than a uniform field of marks. Keep the strongest detail where the viewer should look first.
observation: Compare one rough patch with a smoother area. Notice that the light pattern remains visible beneath both.
steps: Block in the largest stone's form without texture.
Add a small cluster of texture marks near a turning edge.
Hide the guide and leave most of the remaining surface quiet.
check: Does the texture support a focal area?
transfer: Draw a piece of bark with detail in only one small area.

title: A natural history study
subtitle: Compare instead of collecting detail.
idea: A collection page can show differences in shape, scale, and surface. Keep one measuring unit across the objects and use varied levels of detail. A small silhouette study beside a fuller rendering makes the comparisons clearer.
observation: Compare the compact acorn, rounded pebble, and long feather. Use one shared unit to relate their proportions and spacing.
steps: Place three envelopes using one shared unit.
Develop one object fully and describe the other two more simply.
Fade the guide and add a small memory silhouette for each object.
check: Can I explain how the three forms differ?
transfer: Make a study page of three found objects you can legally collect.

title: A landscape in three boxes
subtitle: Plan before the large drawing.
idea: Thumbnail drawings let you test the balance of sky, land, and water quickly. Keep the same small frame and compare alternatives using large masses. Detail cannot repair a weak arrangement as efficiently as a new thumbnail can.
observation: Notice how the near pine, lake, and ridges divide the image. Imagine giving more space to the sky or the shore.
steps: Draw three identical little frames.
Move the horizon and near tree to different positions in each.
Choose one arrangement and redraw its three biggest masses.
check: Is one version clearer about where I should look first?
transfer: Make three thumbnails of a view from your window.

title: Mountains at different distances
subtitle: Use relationships to suggest depth.
idea: Distant land often shows reduced contrast and less visible detail because of the atmosphere. Treat this as an observation to compare in the reference, not a law that every distant object must be pale. Separate the large ridge silhouettes first.
observation: Compare the darker nearby hills and tree masses with the softer far ridges. Their overlaps remain visible where contrast decreases.
steps: Draw the nearest, middle, and far ridge outlines.
Assign a separate contrast range to each distance.
Fade the image and remove unnecessary detail from the farthest ridge.
check: Can I read three distances without relying on labels?
transfer: Sketch a real view and compare its actual near and far contrast.

title: A pine from grouped masses
subtitle: Draw branches as families.
idea: A tree's silhouette is irregular but organized. Group nearby branches into larger masses, then use gaps to separate them. Drawing every needle before the tree's balance is established usually creates noise.
observation: Look for the trunk direction, largest branch groups, and open wedges of sky between them.
steps: Place the trunk gesture and the widest branch reach.
Build three or four large foliage masses.
Hide the guide and suggest a few needles at the edges only.
check: Does the tree feel rooted and balanced?
transfer: Draw a tree outdoors using five foliage masses.

title: Reflections are broken shapes
subtitle: Compare the water with what it reflects.
idea: A reflection can resemble a vertical echo of a subject, but ripples interrupt and stretch it. Observe the actual shapes rather than drawing a perfect upside-down copy. Horizontal accents can suggest the water surface.
observation: Compare the willow and far bank with their softer reflected shapes below. Look for horizontal interruptions along the water.
steps: Lightly map the reflection's overall position.
Group its values into broad broken patches.
Fade the guide and add a few horizontal water marks across those patches.
check: Does the reflection feel part of a flat water surface?
transfer: Observe a reflection in a bowl of water or your own photograph.

title: Near rocks, far ridges
subtitle: Spend detail where it helps.
idea: A strong foreground can anchor a landscape when distant forms stay simpler. Use sharper edges and clearer plane changes near the viewer only where the reference supports them. Avoid outlining the entire horizon with the same heavy line.
observation: Compare the texture of the near rocky shore with the smooth distant silhouette.
steps: Block in both near rocks and far ridges.
Develop three planes on one foreground rock.
Hide the guide and keep the background as a small number of value shapes.
check: Is detail creating depth or covering every area equally?
transfer: Draw a close object with a distant view behind it.

title: Follow the shore into space
subtitle: Use a receding curve.
idea: A shoreline changes direction as it moves away. Its bends can guide the eye through a drawing, but the curve must stay related to the water plane. Place the largest turns before adding small stones.
observation: Follow the cove from the nearest shore to the far headland. Compare how much width each bend occupies.
steps: Mark three major turning points of the shoreline.
Connect them with a broad curve and add the headland.
Fade the image and reduce the whole shore to five segments.
check: Does the route move convincingly away from the viewer?
transfer: Sketch the large bends of a path in a photograph you own.

title: Sky shapes between land
subtitle: Let the negative space guide you.
idea: The sky around a headland is a shape you can compare like any other. Check its width and angle before refining the land. Keeping the sky simple can make the shoreline's silhouette more expressive.
observation: Look at the wedge of sky above the headland and the open band above the horizon.
steps: Draw the sky shape as a flat outline.
Build the headland against that shape.
Hide the guide and make a second crop with more open sky.
check: Does the empty shape help the coastline read?
transfer: Draw a building by first outlining the sky around its roof.

title: Soft clouds, firm land
subtitle: Vary the character of an edge.
idea: An edge can turn gradually or sharply. Compare soft cloud transitions with the firmer silhouette of a rock. Use lighter, interrupted marks for soft boundaries rather than drawing every cloud as a closed cartoon outline.
observation: Compare the pale sky transitions with the darker rocky headland. Look for edges you can barely locate.
steps: Place the major sky and land value groups.
Use firmer marks for selected rock edges and gentle hatching in the sky.
Fade the guide and remove one unnecessary cloud outline.
check: Do the edge choices distinguish atmosphere from solid land?
transfer: Compare a steam cloud and a ceramic cup in your own photograph.

title: Water with fewer marks
subtitle: Keep the surface calm.
idea: A few deliberate horizontal accents can describe calm water. Too many equally strong marks compete with the shore and make the surface feel patterned. Group reflections and reserve quiet paper between them.
observation: Notice the broad quiet water between the far bank and near reeds. Choose only the largest reflected changes and surface accents.
steps: Block the pond and its major reflections as simple value shapes.
Add five short horizontal accents of varied length.
Hide the guide and stop before the water becomes a repeated pattern.
check: Does the quiet area make the shore more readable?
transfer: Draw a calm water surface using no more than ten marks.

title: A landscape with an intention
subtitle: Choose what the view is about.
idea: A landscape study can emphasize distance, light, or the route of a shoreline. Decide which relationship matters, then simplify details that do not support it. Your drawing may legitimately differ from the source when that choice is deliberate.
observation: Follow the rural path from the near tree into the valley. Choose distance, light, or the route as the central relationship in your study.
steps: Write a short intention, then make a thumbnail.
Build the chosen view in three value groups.
Switch to Freehand and make a small variation with a changed crop.
check: Do my strongest marks support the intention I chose?
transfer: Draw a familiar outdoor view with one clear visual priority.

title: Find your eye level
subtitle: Locate the perspective structure.
idea: In a simple one-point view, horizontal edges traveling directly away from you converge toward a point on the horizon. Find that relationship from visible edges. Do not force every line, including vertical edges or unrelated objects, toward the same point.
observation: Compare the long floor edges with the top edges of the hallway. Look for their shared distant direction.
steps: Extend two receding edges lightly toward their meeting point.
Draw an eye-level line through that point.
Fade the reference and block the hallway around those anchors.
check: Do the main receding edges agree on one point?
transfer: Look down a real corridor and estimate its eye level.

title: Floor tiles that recede
subtitle: Compare intervals in depth.
idea: Equal intervals on a floor appear closer together as they recede. Compare the spacing in the image instead of dividing the drawing into equal-height rows. Establish the main perspective rays before placing cross-lines.
observation: The tile rows compress toward the far doorway. The near tiles occupy more of the image.
steps: Draw a few receding floor lines.
Place the near and far transverse divisions by observation.
Fade the guide and add intermediate divisions with gradually smaller spacing.
check: Do the tile rows compress toward the distance?
transfer: Observe paving slabs or floorboards in a photograph you own.

title: A doorway within a doorway
subtitle: Use nested shapes to check proportion.
idea: Nested rectangles can help you compare the depth and size of an interior. Check the far doorway against the opening around it. A small proportional error in a simple rectangle is often easier to spot than one hidden inside detail.
observation: Compare the far door's height with the hallway's back wall and its surrounding margins.
steps: Draw the outer frame of the hallway view.
Place the far opening using its margins as measurements.
Hide the guide and reconstruct the nested shapes at a smaller scale.
check: Are the surrounding spaces proportionate?
transfer: Draw a window and the frame around it as nested shapes.

title: Window light on the floor
subtitle: Keep light attached to a surface.
idea: A patch of light changes shape as it lands on a floor or wall. Its boundaries describe a plane as well as a bright area. Compare the patch with the floor's perspective instead of treating it as a floating rectangle.
observation: Follow the window light across wall and floor. Compare its changing angles with the surface junction and neighboring floorboards.
steps: Establish the floor and wall boundary.
Map the light shape on that floor plane.
Fade the guide and group the surrounding shadow into one broad value.
check: Does the bright shape rest on the floor?
transfer: Observe a real patch of window light before sketching its boundary.

title: An interior without details
subtitle: Make space read with large relationships.
idea: An interior can feel spacious before it has furniture or texture. The enclosing planes, opening, and large light pattern do most of the work. Resist adding objects until the room's proportions are convincing.
observation: Study the ceiling, two walls, floor, and far opening as separate large shapes.
steps: Draw the enclosing planes in five or six strokes.
Add the window and broad light pattern.
Hide the guide and invent a simpler room using the same structure.
check: Can the space read without surface decoration?
transfer: Sketch a corner of your room using fewer than fifteen lines.

title: A door at an angle
subtitle: Compare two directions on a wall.
idea: A wall seen obliquely has receding horizontal edges while verticals remain upright in this level view. Compare top and bottom directions rather than drawing a flat front-facing symbol. Avoid overcompensating with dramatic convergence.
observation: Look at the doorway's top, base, and side reveals. Their visible widths help establish the angle.
steps: Draw the near vertical edge and the top's slope.
Place the far edge and step using their observed widths.
Fade the image and connect the door panels to the same directions.
check: Does the door belong to the wall's plane?
transfer: Draw a cabinet from a gentle three-quarter angle.

title: A step is a small solid
subtitle: Show top, front, and side planes.
idea: A step has thickness and occupies space. Separate its visible planes before adding cracks or worn edges. Small value differences can explain those planes without heavy outlines around every edge.
observation: Compare the step's top surface with its front face and the shadow underneath.
steps: Draw a light box around the step.
Separate its visible planes using three values.
Hide the guide and invent a second step aligned with the first.
check: Can I see a solid step rather than a flat stripe?
transfer: Sketch a closed book as three connected planes.

title: Weathered plaster, quiet marks
subtitle: Let surface detail follow the plane.
idea: Cracks and stains should remain subordinate to the wall's overall shape and lighting. Select a few irregular patches instead of covering the wall with an even texture. Keep the strongest contrast near your chosen focal area.
observation: Compare the quiet broad plaster with the small worn areas near the door and base.
steps: Establish the wall's large value field.
Add three irregular weathering patches with soft boundaries.
Fade the guide and leave at least half the wall free of texture.
check: Does the wall still feel like one continuous plane?
transfer: Draw a worn surface with only five texture accents.

title: A plant pot beside a wall
subtitle: Combine organic and geometric forms.
idea: A pot provides a stable geometric structure while the plant breaks into irregular gestures. Establish the pot's axis, rim, and base before adding the branching silhouette. Compare its contact shadow with the step beside it.
observation: Notice the pot opening and the sparse sapling's direction. Their shapes need different kinds of marks.
steps: Draw the pot as a tapered cylinder.
Add the main stem directions and a few leaf groups.
Hide the guide and connect pot, plant, and ground with selective shadows.
check: Does the plant seem to grow from inside the pot?
transfer: Sketch a houseplant, beginning with its container.

title: An architectural vignette
subtitle: Suggest a place with a few choices.
idea: A vignette can focus on a doorway without drawing an entire building. Let the surroundings become simpler toward the edges of the page. Keep the structural angles accurate where you choose to show them.
observation: The arched blue window, stone sill, and pot offer a compact story of a place. Choose which relationship receives the strongest detail.
steps: Make a small crop around the three main forms.
Check the window, sill, and wall directions before adding tone.
Fade the guide and finish one focal area while letting the margins stay open.
check: Does the vignette feel intentional rather than unfinished everywhere?
transfer: Draw one doorway or window from your own photograph.

title: The head's outer envelope
subtitle: Begin with the whole, not the eye.
idea: A portrait begins with the relationship of the cranium, jaw, neck, and shoulders. Place that envelope before any small features. The outer shape and tilt can carry character even when the face is still empty.
observation: Compare the head's width with its height and the angle of the shoulders. The far side is narrower in this three-quarter view.
steps: Place top, chin, widest point, and neck attachment.
Connect them in a light angular envelope.
Fade the guide and add the hair as a separate large mass.
check: Is the head's tilt clear without features?
transfer: Draw a head from a photograph you have permission to use, starting with the envelope.

title: A centerline that turns
subtitle: Make features belong to the head.
idea: The facial centerline follows the head's turn rather than sitting in the center of the paper shape. Use it to relate the brow, nose, mouth, and chin. Treat common proportion rules as starting checks, then compare the actual face.
observation: Notice how much of each cheek is visible. The nose direction and mouth center belong to the same turn.
steps: Draw the head envelope and curved facial centerline.
Place brow, nose base, and chin along that structure.
Hide the guide and rotate an invented head slightly farther away.
check: Do the features share one turning structure?
transfer: Sketch three simple heads with different centerline directions.

title: Eyes across a curved form
subtitle: Compare alignment before detail.
idea: The eyes sit on a turning head, so the far eye may appear narrower. Establish their alignment and spacing before iris or eyelash detail. Compare the visible shapes rather than drawing two matching eye symbols.
observation: Look at the brow line and the relative widths of the near and far eye. Check the bridge of the nose between them.
steps: Mark the eye line across the head.
Place the two eye shapes and compare the gap.
Fade the reference and add lids with only a few restrained marks.
check: Do the eyes share the same head angle?
transfer: Study the eye alignment in a self-portrait photograph.

title: The nose as a wedge
subtitle: Find planes before nostrils.
idea: A simple wedge can organize the bridge, tip, and side of a nose. Establish its direction and connection to the brow before small dark nostrils. The shadow beside it can explain projection more clearly than an enclosing outline.
observation: Compare the lit bridge with the darker side plane. Notice where the nose overlaps the far cheek.
steps: Draw the nose's main direction and base width.
Separate its top, side, and underside as simple planes.
Fade the image and soften the transitions that are not sharp.
check: Does the nose project without a heavy outline around it?
transfer: Make three small nose studies from a permitted portrait reference.

title: A portrait in light and shadow
subtitle: Preserve the large value design.
idea: The head's light pattern can unite many small features. Start with one shadow family for the cheek, eye socket, and neck where they connect. Keep a few lighter reflected areas inside shadow subordinate to the main light.
observation: Squint at the portrait to see the broad lit and shadowed regions. Hair and clothing are separate local-value decisions.
steps: Draw the head and place the largest shadow boundary.
Fill the shadow family lightly before refining any feature.
Hide the guide and add the strongest accents only near the focal area.
check: Does the face read at thumbnail size?
transfer: Draw a permitted portrait using only three values.

title: The palm as a simple block
subtitle: Give the hand a structure.
idea: The palm is a flexible mass with a broad plane, not a perfect rectangle. Start with its overall wedge and wrist connection. Fingers become easier to place when they attach to an established palm.
observation: Compare the palm's width with its length and the wrist's narrower connection.
steps: Draw a light envelope around palm and wrist.
Mark the knuckle arc and thumb attachment.
Fade the image and connect those anchors without finger details.
check: Does the palm feel connected to the forearm?
transfer: Look at your relaxed hand and sketch its palm as a simple mass.

title: Fingers have a shared gesture
subtitle: Draw the direction before the segments.
idea: Finger segments change direction around joints, but the whole finger has a gesture. Mark that movement before outlining each section. Compare finger lengths and spacing in the actual pose; a relaxed hand rarely has evenly spaced digits.
observation: Follow each finger from its base to its tip. The thumb branches differently from the four fingers.
steps: Draw the palm and five digit gestures.
Place the main joint changes along those gestures.
Hide the guide and add tapered widths around the directions.
check: Do the fingers feel related to one palm?
transfer: Draw your own hand with only gesture lines for each digit.

title: Knuckles on an arc
subtitle: Compare landmarks across the hand.
idea: The finger bases sit along an uneven arc, and the visible joints create additional rhythms. Use those landmarks to compare lengths before adding creases. Do not force every knuckle into one straight row.
observation: Compare the positions of neighboring knuckles and the smaller tip-to-tip changes.
steps: Mark the visible knuckle landmarks as small dots.
Connect each finger's segments between its landmarks.
Fade the guide and refine the outer silhouette while preserving those relationships.
check: Are the joint positions consistent with the fingers' bends?
transfer: Sketch the landmark arcs on your free hand from two views.

title: Shadows between fingers
subtitle: Use the gaps without filling them in.
idea: Dark spaces between fingers can clarify a hand, but an automatic black fill may make the pose rigid. Compare the actual gap shapes and their values. Let one finger's contour stop where another overlaps it.
observation: Study the narrow spaces and the transitions into the palm. Some separations are clear gaps and others are soft shadows.
steps: Draw the three clearest negative shapes.
Build the finger edges around them.
Fade the reference and add only the darkest contact accents.
check: Do the gaps make the hand more readable?
transfer: Sketch your hand resting on a table, starting with its empty spaces.

title: An expressive hand study
subtitle: Let the pose carry the drawing.
idea: A convincing hand study does not require every crease. Decide whether the important quality is openness, tension, or rest, then emphasize the structural relationships that carry it. Use your own hand to check any ambiguous anatomy in a reference.
observation: Compare the palm's broad movement with the quieter finger tips. Choose a focal area rather than detailing every joint equally.
steps: Make a small gesture thumbnail of both hands together.
Develop the palm masses and the most important finger overlaps.
Switch to Freehand and draw your own relaxed hand for comparison.
check: Can the pose read before the small creases?
transfer: Draw two contrasting hand poses from life and describe their mood.

title: A robin in three masses
subtitle: Build body, head, and tail.
idea: A bird can begin as a rounded body mass, a smaller head, and a directional tail. Connect those parts before detailing feathers. Compare their actual proportions; an oversized head or tail changes the bird's character quickly.
observation: Find the body oval's tilt and the head's position relative to it. The tail continues a different direction.
steps: Draw the three masses with light strokes.
Connect the neck and wing silhouette around them.
Fade the image and refine the outer contour without feather detail.
check: Does the bird read as one connected form?
transfer: Reduce a bird in your own photo to three masses.

title: The folded wing as a shape
subtitle: Separate the wing from the body.
idea: A folded wing is a large overlapping shape before it becomes individual feathers. Its upper edge and tapered tip help explain how it lies against the torso. Keep the body volume underneath it.
observation: Compare the wing's long shape with the rounder breast. Look at where its edge disappears into plumage.
steps: Place the body oval and wing envelope.
Mark the wing tip and the main overlap edge.
Hide the guide and suggest only two feather groups inside the wing.
check: Does the wing rest on the body rather than replace it?
transfer: Study the folded wing of another bird from a permitted photo.

title: A beak and an eye in place
subtitle: Use small landmarks sparingly.
idea: Small dark features attract attention, so place them after checking the head's silhouette and turn. Compare the eye-to-beak distance and the beak's direction. A tiny misplaced accent can change the apparent gaze.
observation: Look at the eye's position inside the head mass and the beak's relation to the forehead.
steps: Draw the head envelope without details.
Mark the eye location and beak direction lightly.
Fade the reference and add the compact dark accents once.
check: Does the gaze follow the head's direction?
transfer: Make three tiny bird heads with different gaze directions.

title: Feet that grip a branch
subtitle: Explain contact and balance.
idea: A perched bird's weight passes through its legs to the branch. Observe the visible toes and where they wrap around the support rather than drawing generic hooks. Omit hidden toes instead of inventing extra visible ones.
observation: Compare the feet's contact points with the body's center. Notice the branch's thickness beneath the grip.
steps: Draw the branch and the two leg directions.
Place the visible toe curves around the branch.
Fade the image and relate the feet to the body above.
check: Does the bird seem supported by the branch?
transfer: Observe a bird photo and mark its support points before drawing.

title: Feathers as directional groups
subtitle: Suggest plumage with restraint.
idea: Feather texture works best when grouped by direction and value. Individual tiny marks should follow the rounded breast or folded wing. Preserve quiet areas so the bird's large form does not disappear into repeated strokes.
observation: Compare the soft breast with the more structured wing. Their marks need different lengths and directions.
steps: Shade the bird's broad light and shadow families.
Add short curved groups on the breast and longer accents on the wing.
Hide the guide and leave the lit silhouette mostly quiet.
check: Can I see volume before feather texture?
transfer: Draw a small feather using only its axis and grouped barbs.

title: A resting cat's silhouette
subtitle: Find the complete pose.
idea: A curled or resting animal can hide many anatomical parts. Begin with the full silhouette and its large internal divisions. Do not add limbs simply because you know they should exist; draw the parts actually visible.
observation: Compare the cat's rounded torso with the smaller head and the sweep of the tail.
steps: Mark the pose's highest, lowest, and widest points.
Connect a simple envelope and place the head mass.
Fade the guide and refine the visible silhouette without fur.
check: Does the resting pose read as a whole?
transfer: Sketch a resting pet from life before it changes position.

title: The cat's head as a solid
subtitle: Place ears and muzzle on a mass.
idea: A cat's skull has width, depth, and a projecting muzzle. Place the facial center direction and ear bases before pointed ear tips. Compare the actual ear spacing instead of attaching two identical triangles to a circle.
observation: Look at the head turn, the muzzle's projection, and the different visible ear shapes.
steps: Draw the head mass and center direction.
Place the muzzle wedge and broad ear bases.
Fade the guide and add the eye line with a few small accents.
check: Do the ears and muzzle belong to the same head turn?
transfer: Study an animal head from a photograph you own.

title: Fur follows the body
subtitle: Make texture reveal a turning form.
idea: Fur changes direction across an animal. Group it into broad flows, then use a few small accents to suggest softness. A continuous sawtooth outline makes every edge equally busy and can obscure the underlying pose.
observation: Compare fur direction on the cheek, shoulder, and flank. Look for smoother patches between tufts.
steps: Draw the body's main light and dark shapes.
Add three groups of marks following the fur's direction.
Hide the guide and interrupt the silhouette with only a few tufts.
check: Does the fur support the body's shape?
transfer: Draw a furry object with most texture confined to one area.

title: Where the animal's weight rests
subtitle: Look for support and compression.
idea: A resting animal contacts a surface across several areas. Flattened shapes and small contact shadows suggest weight. Compare those compressed areas with the rounder upper body instead of shading everything equally.
observation: Notice where the cat meets its support and where the belly or limbs disappear into overlap.
steps: Outline the major support contacts.
Shade the compact contact shadows beneath them.
Fade the image and keep the upper body transitions softer.
check: Does the cat feel settled on the surface?
transfer: Draw a cushion with an object pressing into it.

title: Character without caricature
subtitle: Choose one telling relationship.
idea: An animal's character can emerge from its head tilt, silhouette, or resting rhythm. Choose one of those relationships to emphasize while keeping its structure credible. More whiskers rarely fix a weak pose.
observation: Compare the brown dog’s head tilt with the quieter resting body and paws. Choose the structural relationship that communicates its attentive character.
steps: Make two tiny gesture thumbnails of the dog with different crops.
Choose one and develop its silhouette and support.
Switch to Freehand and create a small variation of the pose.
check: Which structural choice carries the animal's character?
transfer: Draw the same pet twice: once for movement and once for rest.

title: A courtyard in thumbnails
subtitle: Design a route for the eye.
idea: A small courtyard combines architecture, plants, and open ground. Establish the large arrangement before deciding which pot or leaf deserves attention. Thumbnail studies let you move the emphasis without laboring over details.
observation: Compare the doorway, plant groups, and open paving as large shapes. Look for a route from near to far.
steps: Draw two small frames with different crops.
Block the largest light and dark masses in each.
Choose one and mark a focal area with a compact accent.
check: Can I follow a clear route through the composition?
transfer: Make two thumbnails of a familiar outdoor corner.

title: Foliage against plaster
subtitle: Balance detail with empty wall.
idea: A leafy silhouette can be expressive against a quiet wall. Compare the negative gaps and group the leaves into larger clusters. The surrounding empty surface gives those clusters room to read.
observation: Find one large foliage mass and three sky or wall gaps inside it. Compare their different sizes.
steps: Draw the outside foliage envelope.
Cut three negative gaps into that envelope.
Fade the guide and add detail to only one cluster.
check: Does the empty wall help the foliage stand out?
transfer: Sketch a houseplant against a plain background.

title: Pots as a family of forms
subtitle: Repeat with variation.
idea: Repeated objects can create rhythm when their heights, widths, and spacing vary. Align their contact points to the ground and compare their ellipses. Repetition does not mean copying the same pot shape several times.
observation: Compare the courtyard pots' scale and distance. Notice where one interrupts another.
steps: Place the largest and smallest pot envelopes.
Add the remaining pots using the gaps as measurements.
Hide the guide and invent a new group with varied spacing.
check: Is the rhythm varied while the ground remains coherent?
transfer: Arrange three containers and draw their silhouette rhythm.

title: A path through the picture
subtitle: Connect the foreground and background.
idea: Receding paving and overlapping objects can guide attention through a scene. Choose the strongest route and simplify competing lines. The route should stay consistent with the ground plane rather than become a decorative stripe.
observation: Follow the paving toward the far doorway. Compare the width of near and far intervals.
steps: Draw the ground's broad perspective direction.
Place a few paving divisions and object contact points.
Fade the guide and strengthen only the lines that support the route.
check: Does the route lead toward my focal area?
transfer: Draw a path in your own photo using only five guiding lines.

title: Color translated into value
subtitle: Compare lightness before naming color.
idea: Different colors can share a similar value, and the same color can span many values in light and shadow. Use the monochrome reference view to check your first impression. Build a value design that survives without color.
observation: Compare terracotta, foliage, and plaster in color, then turn on Monochrome. Notice which boundaries become less obvious.
steps: Make a three-value thumbnail before changing the view.
Switch to Monochrome and revise the largest mismatch.
Hide the guide and preserve that value plan in a new sketch.
check: Which color relationship surprised me in monochrome?
transfer: Compare a colorful scene and its grayscale photograph.

title: Two wheels, one viewpoint
subtitle: Align the bicycle's large circles.
idea: A bicycle starts with two wheels and their shared contact with the ground. Depending on the camera angle, the wheels may appear as ellipses. Compare their centers, apparent sizes, and tilt before drawing spokes.
observation: Look at the two wheels and the line between their contact points. Treat them as observed shapes rather than automatic perfect circles.
steps: Mark the wheel centers and ground contacts.
Draw the two outer wheel shapes with light strokes.
Fade the image and check the wheelbase against wheel height.
check: Do both wheels belong to one viewpoint and ground plane?
transfer: Sketch a parked bicycle from your own photograph.

title: A frame made of angles
subtitle: Build the structure before components.
idea: A bicycle frame can be simplified into a few connected segments and triangular gaps. Compare those angles before adding handlebars, chain, or cables. Correcting one triangle can bring several connected parts into alignment.
observation: Study the main frame triangle and the fork direction. Look at the empty spaces they enclose.
steps: Draw the largest frame triangle between the wheel centers.
Add the fork and seat direction using observed angles.
Hide the guide and rebuild the same frame with fewer lines.
check: Are the triangular gaps proportionate?
transfer: Block in the frame of a chair using straight segments.

title: Spokes behind the frame
subtitle: Choose what overlaps and what disappears.
idea: Complex mechanical subjects become clearer when you establish the overlap order. The frame passes in front of some wheel details, while nearer parts cover farther ones. You do not need every spoke to make a wheel readable.
observation: Find places where the frame interrupts the wheels. Compare visible and hidden portions of the far side.
steps: Draw the main wheel and frame silhouettes.
Add only a few spokes that explain each wheel's center.
Fade the image and stop hidden lines at the correct overlaps.
check: Can I explain the front-to-back order of the parts?
transfer: Draw a wire object while omitting all hidden segments.

title: Tell a story with a crop
subtitle: Let the frame make a choice.
idea: A crop can emphasize the bicycle as an object or the place around it. Compare a close mechanical study with a wider environmental view. Keep essential support and contact information even when parts leave the frame.
observation: Consider the bicycle's relationship to the wall and paving. Decide whether the subject is the machine or the quiet place.
steps: Draw one close crop and one wider thumbnail.
Choose the version that supports your intended story.
Switch to Freehand and develop only its important shapes and values.
check: Does the crop communicate the subject I chose?
transfer: Photograph a personal object in its usual setting and test two crops.

title: A small portfolio, a next step
subtitle: Look back and choose deliberately.
idea: Progress becomes visible through comparison. Revisit an early study and a recent one, describe a specific change, and choose a practical next exercise. A portfolio is a considered selection, not a requirement that every drawing be finished.
observation: Use the reference as a starting point for a personal final study. Combine your own crop with the skills you now find useful.
steps: Draw one final study of this scene or a personal reference photo.
Compare it with an early saved drawing in My practice.
Write one observed improvement and one precise goal for your next week.
check: Can I name a visible change instead of judging the whole drawing?
transfer: Select three exported studies and plan a new subject to draw from life.
